# Data, Annotation, and Ground Truth {#sec-data-annotation}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The experiments were run on the Turkish
product-review corpus of chapter 4 and on its 40,000/10,000 train/test split
(@sec-bake-off); in some experiments the size or the labels of the training
subset were changed. The computations used `scikit-learn` 1.9.0, NumPy 2.5.2
and pandas 3.0.5 on Python 3.12.13. Two results are hand audits: one person,
with the criteria written down before the reading began, read 100 randomly
selected test reviews and a separate 40 test reviews that the model disputed
most strongly. Those counts rest on that reader's judgement and were not
checked by a second human annotator.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- read a sample of your own data and classify what you find into label errors, schema problems, and model errors — and act differently on each;
- write an annotation guideline that two independent people can apply, one that spells out the ambiguous cases and a `SKIP` option;
- compute raw inter-annotator agreement and Cohen's kappa, and explain why a raw agreement as high as 93% is not enough without the class distribution;
- measure label noise by class and by direction, and assess its effect with a controlled experiment;
- audit your splits for leaks and, when a leak is found, report how the measurement changes.

## The number you have been trusting

Round 2 of @sec-bake-off ranked seven representations in one table. Tf-idf over word 1–2 grams, fed to a balanced logistic regression, scored **92.57% accuracy and 76.21 macro-F1**. Bag of words scored 73.51. Averaged word2vec scored 61.39. The chapter's conclusion was that, *on that data and with those settings*, the sparse representations were well ahead of the from-scratch averaged embeddings, by far more than the sampling uncertainty of the test set. The order of neighbouring rows, though, was sensitive to the tuning budget: raw counts and TF-IDF swapped places once `C` was chosen on validation. So trying a strong sparse baseline first is a good start; a general claim that one method is better takes new data and a new uncertainty analysis.

::: {#gloss-gold-standard .column-margin .term-gloss}
**gold standard** — the labels treated as correct when a model is scored.
They may come from adjudication, from an expert's decision or from another
documented process. Being the reference does not make them free of error;
their provenance and the disagreements inside them have to be examined
separately. [↩](#term-gold-standard){.term-back}
:::

Every one of those numbers was computed by comparing the model's output against a column called `sentiment`. Throughout this chapter we call the labels in that column the **reference labels**: they are the point of reference for evaluation, not a claim to be the one indisputable reading of the text. The terms [gold standard](#gloss-gold-standard){#term-gold-standard .term-ref} and *ground truth* name the same function. Who produced the labels, in answer to which question and how, is not documented; in the previous chapter we did not ask once.

This chapter asks. In some of the experiments we hold chapter 4's highest-scoring representation, the classifier and the test reviews fixed and change only the training labels or the test labels. In others the amount of labelled training data, the selection of examples or the split itself changes too; each table says which components stay fixed. That way a change in score is interpreted only inside the controlled comparison of its own table.

What comes out is uncomfortable. A 2% error rate in the *test* labels drags the leaderboard's top entry below the score its bag-of-words rival earned on *clean* labels — not because the model changed, but because the ruler did. Note the shape of that comparison, because it is the honest one: two conditions with differently labelled test sets, not a rank reversal on a shared one. Scoring both models on the same noisy labels would answer a different question, and this chapter does not answer it. Of the **40 selected test reviews** the model disputed most strongly, 20 were classified as texts that a single binary label struggles to describe; that proportion cannot be carried over to the dataset as a whole. And 1,000 clean labels tie with 40,000 labels at 10% noise; at 20% noise, 500 clean labels beat all 40,000.

::: {.column-margin}
The corpus is the same one as in chapter 4 (@sec-bake-off): 235,165 Turkish product reviews, about 93.7% of them labelled positive. That imbalance strongly shapes many of the results; the schema, the model and the sampling decisions are part of the results too.
:::

**What we will look at.** First the steps through which labels are produced,
and a hand audit of a hundred random reviews. Then annotator agreement, the
limits of the schema, label noise and leaks between the splits, each with its
own experiment. The last sections cover the annotation budget and the
alternatives to labelling by hand.

## Where a label actually comes from

Labels do not arise by themselves. First the categories and the decision rules are set; then texts are selected, annotators decide, and disagreements are merged. At each step the meaning of the label can drift from what you assume; and if the steps were not recorded, you cannot tell which decision produced the final label.

The stored label gathers into one column every decision made from the selection of the text to the merging of disagreements; your training run, your leaderboard and your production monitoring see only that column. The 20/40 and 11/40 in the figure belong only to the single-reader audit of the 40 test reviews the model disputed most strongly; how often the problems at the other stages occur was not measured in this chapter.
:::

::::

The last box is the one to watch. When a dataset is distributed with only a text column and a `label` column, the history of the annotators' decisions becomes invisible: disagreements, hard cases and skipped examples are reduced to a single integer. Keeping the disagreements, the hard cases, the skipped examples and the adjudication decisions as well — in extra columns, in a dump of the individual judgements, or in a datasheet — gives a dataset that can be audited far better than a single integer can.

### The questions to ask before you use a dataset

Before any modelling, try to answer the six questions below. Record what the source does not say as "undocumented", and assess separately what that uncertainty means for your decision to use the data.

1. **Who produced the text?** Not "the internet". Which platform, which population, which time window. The review corpus is people who chose to write a review after a purchase, which is not the same population as people who bought.
2. **Who produced the labels, and how?** It may be domain experts, crowdworkers, a model, or the platform's star rating. Deriving a sentiment class from a star rating is a **proxy labelling** decision: it carries the rating scale's own biases, and how well the stars match the sentiment question you are targeting has to be tested. Crowdsourced labels are not automatically worse than expert ones: @snow2008cheap showed that on some tasks the combined judgements of a handful of non-experts can match expert quality. That result is not guaranteed for every task or every way of combining; it depends on the task being one a non-expert can answer at all.
3. **What question were they answering?** "Is this review positive?" and "Would you buy this product?" and "Is this customer satisfied?" produce different labels on the same text.
4. **What licence, and does it cover your use?** Research-only is a real restriction. So is a licence that permits redistribution of the text but not of derived models.
5. **What legal basis and what notice existed for the use?** That anyone can read a review does not show that explicit consent to model training was given. Examine separately the platform's terms, the purpose the data was processed for, and the legal basis that could apply.
6. **What is missing?** Which texts were deleted, filtered, or never written, and which groups does that affect? This is the hardest one and the one most worth attempting. @dodge2021documenting did it for C4, one of the most-used web corpora in the field, and showed that the blocklist used to "clean" it had disproportionately left out text about and by minority groups. Selection of this kind cannot be seen from the distributed data alone; it takes a record of the collection and filtering decisions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Licensing: what an engineer needs to know

Before any of that, a question that can stop a project after it ships rather
than before it starts: are you allowed to use this data at all?

**Public does not mean free to use.** "I could download it" and "I am permitted to train on it" are different claims. Being able to access content does not mean permission to redistribute it or to train a model on it has been documented. Scraped-from-the-web corpora frequently carry no licence at all. Examine the source's licence, the platform's terms and the rights in the content separately, for your own intended use.

**Assess separately what the data licence means for the model.** Which obligations a licence such as CC BY-NC-SA creates for training, for distributing a model or for the outputs it generates is not settled by an automatic "the licence travels" rule; it can vary with the jurisdiction and with how much of the data the model memorises. This is unsettled law. Examine the licence text, your form of use and the relevant jurisdiction for your concrete case, and be conservative in anything you ship.

**Document the provenance.** Record, at minimum: the source URL, the access and download dates, the licence text, the data version or a file hash, the exact filtering you applied, and your splitting decisions. @longpre2024audit audited 1,800+ popular text datasets and found licence information missing or wrong for a large fraction of them — including datasets used in production. What you did not record at download time becomes hard to reconstruct later.

**Assess personal data and data governance separately.** If a review makes its writer identifiable, directly or indirectly, a personal-data regime applies alongside copyright. Consent is not the only legal basis: KVKK Article 5(2)(d) allows processing data the person has made public themselves. But that basis is read narrowly and is limited to the purpose for which the person made the data public; a review posted to inform other shoppers does not automatically become model-training material. Erasure requests — KVKK Articles 7 and 11 in Turkey, GDPR Article 17 in the EU — are assessed within the conditions and exceptions of those articles; "I already trained on it" is not, by itself, an answer. Meeting a request takes the row-id-to-source mapping; because that mapping can itself carry personal data, keep it for as long as needed and with security measures. And if the system you build is **high-risk** under the EU AI Act, check the obligations of its Article 10 on the governance of training, validation and test data as well: documented provenance, examination for bias, and a stated data-governance process. For the obligations and their dates see @sec-governance-kvkk.
:::

## Read a hundred rows. Yourself. {#sec-random-audit}

Early in a data project, reading a randomly selected sample by hand is a useful audit that needs no code beyond drawing the sample. Set time aside for it: draw 100 rows from your test set, read them with the label visible, and record the ambiguities and the outright label contradictions you see separately.

I drew 100 rows from the 10,000-row test split with seed 42 (`np.random.default_rng(42).choice(10000, 100, replace=False)`) and read all of them. The criteria were fixed before reading:

- **error** — the gold label contradicts the text;
- **undecidable** — a single binary label is not determined by the text;
- **ok** — everything else.

I split `ok` in two during the reading, which is a deviation from the
pre-registered scheme and is recorded here for exactly that reason:
**arguable** for rows where the gold label is defensible but I would have chosen
the other one, and plain `ok` for the rest. The `arguable` count is therefore a
post-hoc category and carries less weight than the other three.

The result:

```text
### random 100 test rows, read by hand by one reader

errors (gold contradicts the text)          0
undecidable (binary label not determined)   7
   ... of which "not yet received"          3
arguable (post-hoc; defensible either way)  9
ok (the remaining rows)                    84
                                          ---
                                          100
positive gold labels in the sample         98
```

Zero outright errors in 100 draws. With zero hits, the rule of three gives an approximate one-sided 95% upper confidence bound of 3/n: the data are **consistent with an error rate up to about 3%**, and rule nothing below that out. It is not a measurement that the rate is under 3%, and 100 draws cannot distinguish 0.1% from 2%. If a uniform prior (Beta(1,1)) is chosen, the posterior mean for zero outright errors in 100 rows is $1/(n+2) = 1/102 \approx 0.98\%$. That value does not mean the error rate of the corpus has been measured as 1%: it depends on the choice of prior and on one reader's definition of an "outright error". In later calculations we use about 1% only as an example scenario. The seven undecidable rows and the nine arguable ones are not part of this count of outright errors.

The seven undecidable rows are the interesting ones, because they are not errors. Test row 4745 reads, in full:

> `sipariş verdim umarım tez ulaşır :)` — "I placed the order, hope it arrives fast :)"

Gold label: positive. The reviewer has not received the product; there is no product verdict in the text, only a smiley and an expression of hope. Under the schema proposed in this chapter, which targets *the verdict on the product*, this review is undecidable. Because it is not documented which question the original `sentiment` label answered, we do not call the source label of this row an error. Two of the other six are the same shape ("I just ordered it, judging by the reviews…", "it will probably arrive tomorrow"). One arrived used and scratched, but the reviewer says the product itself is good — a verdict on the *delivery* pointing the opposite way from the verdict on the *product*. Of the remaining three, one is a proverb about doors, one offers only a suggestion ("it would be better in liquid form"), and one is the string `seat leon st 1.6tdi` and nothing else.

When the target is *a binary verdict on the product*, these seven rows fit a single label poorly. The problem may lie in the definition of the target question rather than in a wrong decision by the source annotator; confirming that would take the original schema and a second reader's decisions. Hold onto this distinction between a label error and a schema problem; the rest of the chapter keeps returning to it.

::: {.column-margin}
Ninety-eight of the hundred were positive, against a corpus rate of 93.7%. That is borderline but still explainable by sampling noise for n = 100 (at a 6.3% negative rate, the chance of at most 2 negatives in 100 rows is about 4.5%), but it is a reminder that a 100-row sample of a skewed corpus tells you almost nothing about the minority class. To audit the minority class, sample it separately.
:::

## The schema can do as much damage as the annotators

To look into whether the limits of the schema show up on a larger body of data, we can set up a screening rule. The contrastive-connective test below does not diagnose a schema problem; it selects reviews to re-read.

To search 10,000 reviews for candidate contrasts, mark the words *ama*, *fakat*, *ancak* and *lakin* — all roughly "but". Whether a matching review really contains two opposed evaluations cannot be known without checking by hand.

A caveat the rest of this section rests on: this is a screen, not a parser, and
its precision is unmeasured. *Ancak* also means "only" or "barely" — *ancak 3
günde geldi* is a statement about delivery time, not a contrast — and the rule
misses *gerçi*, *ne var ki* and *buna rağmen* entirely. So the 20.03% found
below is neither an upper nor a lower bound; it is only the match rate of the
rule. Reading randomly selected matches would measure the rule's precision;
for the contrasts it misses, the non-matching reviews have to be examined too.
We checked the part that can be checked mechanically: the ambiguous *ancak*
occurs in 351 reviews, 287 of which match through *ancak* alone, and with
*ancak* taken out of the rule the gap between the two groups of the table
below stays in place (macro-F1 71.29 against 77.80). Attributing the score gap
between the two groups to the schema takes a more detailed annotation.

```python
import re
# tr_lower is the Turkish-aware lowercaser from chapter 4 (İ->i, I->ı)
CONTRAST = re.compile(r"\b(ama|fakat|ancak|lakin)\b")
has_but = np.array([bool(CONTRAST.search(tr_lower(t))) for t in test.text])
```

**In 2,003 of the 10,000 test reviews (20.03%) at least one of the four connectives matched.** The class distribution and the model scores of this group are compared with the non-matching group below:

| | contrast rule matches | no match |
|:---|---:|---:|
| share of test set | 20.03% | 79.97% |
| gold negative rate | 11.48% | 5.03% |
| model accuracy | 84.07 | 94.70 |
| model macro-F1 | 72.11 | 77.72 |
| model F1 (negative) | 53.84 | 58.27 |

: The same model, the same test set, split by the four-connective screening rule {tbl-colwidths="[40,30,30]"}

This fifth of the test set has more than twice the negative rate (11.48% against 5.03%), and the model scores clearly lower on it: 5.6 points lower macro-F1 and 4.4 points lower negative-class F1 (the bootstrap interval of the macro-F1 gap over the test rows runs from 2.5 to 8.8 points). The ten-point accuracy gap overstates this: the two groups have different base rates, so part of any accuracy difference comes from the class mix alone. This measurement does not separate the possible explanations. The label schema may be being asked to compress two verdicts into one bit; the model may be making more mistakes on these sentences; and the two groups differ in other respects too — the matching reviews are clearly longer (median 30 tokens against 16). Because no aspect-level re-annotation was done (product, delivery, price and so on labelled separately), we cannot choose between the schema explanation and the model explanation. A sample in which the product, delivery and price verdicts are labelled separately is what it takes to test which error comes from which source: if the model recovers both aspects correctly and only the single bit is wrong, the problem is in the schema.

Which fix applies follows from which explanation holds, so the aspect-level annotation above is what decides it. If the disagreement comes from the target definition, the fix is a richer schema (aspect-level labels: product / delivery / price / packaging, each with its own polarity) or an explicit rule in the guideline telling every annotator which clause wins. If it comes from the model reading these sentences badly, a better representation is exactly what helps — and nothing here rules that out.

A related problem has a name: **annotation artifacts** — the labelling process creating a cue between text and label that lies outside the target task. When a guideline pushes annotators toward a habit, models can learn the habit instead of the task, and the score is usually pushed *up*. @gururangan2018annotation showed that a well-known inference benchmark could be partly solved by reading the hypothesis sentence alone and ignoring the premise entirely: the annotators who wrote those sentences had tells, and the model found them. The connective match here is something else: it defines a candidate group for schema problems and model errors; by itself it is not evidence of an artifact or of a schema flaw in this data. What the two situations share is that a label can reflect the labelling process as well as the text.

@geva2019annotator showed, in a data setup where the annotators wrote the examples themselves, that models can identify *which annotator* wrote an item, and that scores drop when the test set comes from annotators not seen in training. A setup in which ready-made product reviews are only handed out for labelling is different. This corpus has no author or annotator identifiers, so the size of any such effect cannot be measured here.

### What a usable guideline looks like

::: {#gloss-annotation-guideline .column-margin .term-gloss}
**annotation guideline** — the document that sets out in writing the task,
the classes, the decided examples and how ambiguous cases are to be handled.
It makes the decisions of independent annotators more consistent and easier
to audit; it does not guarantee full agreement. [↩](#term-annotation-guideline){.term-back}
:::

In an [annotation guideline](#gloss-annotation-guideline){#term-annotation-guideline .term-ref} the class definitions are only the start. For independent annotators to decide consistently on borderline cases it also needs decided examples, priority rules and a `SKIP` option. Keep the guideline together with the version number of those decisions.

```text
### annotation guideline v1 — product review sentiment

TASK
  Label each review positive (1) or negative (0) according to the
  reviewer's verdict ON THE PRODUCT.

DECIDED CASES  (these make the definition above concrete)
  1. Delivery, packaging, seller, and returns are NOT the product.
     "Fast shipping, product is useless"          -> 0
     "Shipping was late, the product is great"    -> 1
  2. Price complaints are NOT negative unless the reviewer says the
     product is not worth it.
     "Expensive but excellent"                    -> 1
     "Not worth this money"                       -> 0
  3. Mixed verdicts on the product: the FINAL clause wins.
     "Cuts well but the handle broke"             -> 0
     "The handle is cheap but it cuts very well"  -> 1
  4. Not yet received / no verdict given          -> SKIP (do not label)
  5. Truncated text: if the visible text contains a verdict, label it;
     otherwise SKIP.
    6. Judge negation in context. "fena değil" (not bad) is positive
     for the product. "fena değil ama çabuk bozuldu" (not bad but it
     broke quickly) is 0 by rule 3, because the final verdict on the
     product is negative.

WHEN TO SKIP
    If no decision about the product can be made, choose SKIP. Keep the
  skipped examples and the reason; they help improve the guideline and
  the schema. A forced binary label can measure the wrong target even
  when it looks consistent.
```

Two properties make this usable. First, every decided case has a worked example on both sides, so an annotator matching by pattern gets it right without understanding the principle. Second, `SKIP` exists. Forcing a binary choice on undecidable items can manufacture disagreement you will later blame on the annotators; and if the annotators guess by the same habit, it can also manufacture an agreement that looks high and means little.

::: {.column-margin}
The choice in rule 3 — "the final clause wins" — is arbitrary. It can give consistency; whether it really represents satisfaction with the product has to be tested separately. Settle the target question first, then write a *decidable and consistent* rule for the hard cases: an annotator must always be able to tell which rule applies, and to apply it the same way every time. An arbitrary rule applied consistently produces learnable data, and a principled rule applied inconsistently does not. But good agreement does not make a shared answer to the wrong target correct.
:::

## Agreement: what does 93% tell you by itself? {#agreement-and-why-93-of-it-can-be-worthless}

The hundred-row audit showed one reader's decisions. Having an independent second person label the same reviews shows how hard it is to agree on the borderline cases. The agreement figure, though, has to be read together with the class distribution and the table of disagreements; this section explains why.

::: {#gloss-inter-annotator-agreement-iaa .column-margin .term-gloss}
**inter-annotator agreement (IAA)** — the extent to which the decisions of
people labelling the same items independently coincide. It can be summarised
by the raw rate, by class-specific agreement or by chance-corrected
coefficients. High agreement does not by itself prove that the labels
represent the target concept correctly. [↩](#term-inter-annotator-agreement-iaa){.term-back}
:::

You cannot know your labels are good by looking at one annotator's output. You need a second opinion on the same items, and a number for how often the two opinions match — the [inter-annotator agreement](#gloss-inter-annotator-agreement-iaa){#term-inter-annotator-agreement-iaa .term-ref}.

I had no second human annotator, so to have something to compare the reference column with I used a lexicon rule: 36 positive and 37 negative phrases, applied to all 10,000 test rows. The phrase lists are not printed on this page; so the 2×2 table below cannot be reproduced from the code shown, while every coefficient derived from the table can.

One caveat before the numbers, because it changes what the coefficient means.
B is not an independent second opinion in the sense inter-annotator agreement
requires: the rule was written by someone who had already seen the reference
labels. In this table $\kappa(\text{A}, \text{B})$ summarises the **overlap**
between the reference labels and the lexicon rule; it is not a measure of
human–human agreement or of whether the schema is well defined. The same
formula and the same arithmetic — prevalence, $p_e$, skew — apply to a table
of two humans' judgements; but the sampling and independence conditions of
that experiment have to be set up separately. The number 0.2698 belongs only
to this reference-versus-rule table and should not be quoted as a human–human
agreement figure.

```python
def annotator_b(text):
    t = tr_lower(text)
    neg = any(p in t for p in NEG)
    pos = any(p in t for p in POS)
    if neg and not pos:
        return 0
        return 1          # no match, or matches of both kinds: positive
```

The rule looks for the phrases as **substrings**; it does not check word boundaries, and it says positive when a review contains both a positive and a negative phrase. Switching to a rule with word boundaries would mean recomputing the table below.

A is the reference `sentiment` column of the dataset; B is the output of the lexicon rule above. For brevity we call both "annotators", but neither is a human reading the text independently. The table comparing these two label sequences on the 10,000 test reviews:

```text
### A (gold, rows) vs B (lexicon rule, columns), n = 10,000

                B: negative   B: positive
A: negative           141           491
A: positive           167          9201
```

Raw agreement is $(141 + 9201)/10000 = \mathbf{93.42\%}$. But 9,201 of that total are shared positive decisions: the majority class pulls the overall agreement up. To see the disagreement on the negative labels you have to look at the first row and the first column of the table separately.

::: {#gloss-cohen-s-kappa .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Cohen's kappa** — a coefficient that compares the observed agreement of two
label sequences with the agreement expected if each decided independently at
its own label rates. A low kappa is not, by itself, evidence of label errors
or of carelessness. [↩](#term-cohen-s-kappa){.term-back}
:::

The 93.42% raw agreement is not strong evidence by itself. If the decisions are assumed to be made **independently of each other** under the marginals of these two label sequences, the expected agreement is about 90.99%. That is a mathematical reference value; it does not mean the rule, or real annotators, did not read the texts. Nor does a low kappa against a lexicon show that the reference labels are wrong. [Cohen's kappa](#gloss-cohen-s-kappa){#term-cohen-s-kappa .term-ref} [@cohen1960coefficient] compares these two rates:

$$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}$$

where $p_o$ is the observed agreement and $p_e$ is the agreement expected if both annotators labelled independently at their own base rates. Here $p_e = 0.9099$, and:

$$\kappa = \frac{0.9342 - 0.9099}{1 - 0.9099} = \mathbf{0.2698}$$

Krippendorff's alpha [@krippendorff2018content], which handles more than two annotators and missing values, gives 0.2655 on the same table. Its closeness to kappa is not an independent confirmation: the two coefficients are computed from the same label pairs. Because they define expected agreement differently, they will come clearly apart on the balanced subsample below.

A kappa of 0.27 is, on the conventional (and arbitrary) scales, "fair". The useful reading is a comparison rather than a decomposition: **93.42 points of observed agreement against 90.99 that two annotators with these marginals would reach while labelling independently, leaving 2.43 points above that baseline.** Resist turning that into "90.99 points *were* chance": $p_e$ is the agreement expected under an independence null, not a measurable portion of what actually happened. A low kappa on a corpus this skewed is consistent with careless labelling and with careful labelling alike; the coefficient does not tell you which one you have.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The arithmetic of $p_e$, spelled out

That correction is doing all the work, so it is worth seeing exactly what it
computes rather than taking the number on trust.

$p_e$ is the share of agreement expected when the observed class rates of the two label sequences are kept and the decisions are assumed to be independent of each other. The calculation rests on how often each sequence uses the negative and the positive label.

Annotator A calls 632/10000 = 6.32% of items negative. Annotator B calls 308/10000 = 3.08% negative. So:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_e &= P(\text{both say negative}) + P(\text{both say positive}) \\
    &= (0.0632)(0.0308) + (0.9368)(0.9692) \\
    &= 0.00195 + 0.90795 \\
    &= 0.90989
\end{aligned}
$$

Almost all of $p_e$ — 0.908 of 0.910 — comes from the second term. Do the arithmetic with the real marginals rather than a round number, because the round number misleads: A calls 93.68% positive and B 96.92%, and two labellers with those rates, choosing independently, land on the same answer $0.9368 \times 0.9692 + 0.0632 \times 0.0308 = 0.910$ of the time *whatever the texts say*. (Two labellers at 90% would reach $0.9^2 + 0.1^2 = 0.82$, not 0.90 — the expected agreement is not the marginal.) Kappa's denominator, $1 - p_e = 0.09$, is the room left for genuine agreement, and the numerator, 0.0243, is how much of that room the annotators actually filled.

This is why kappa comes out low on skewed tasks and why reporting raw agreement *alone* on a skewed task is misleading. It is also why kappa is volatile there: in this table $1 - p_e$ is about 0.09, so **if the marginals are assumed fixed**, a small change in the observed agreement is multiplied by about eleven on its way into kappa. When a cell really changes, the marginals and $p_e$ move as well. Report raw agreement, class-specific agreement, kappa and the confusion table together, and let the reader see the skew.

Cohen's kappa is defined for exactly two annotators. When you have three or more — the normal case once a crowd platform is involved — use Fleiss' kappa [@fleiss1971measuring], which is the generalisation of *Scott's pi* rather than of Cohen's: it computes $p_e$ from a **single marginal pooled across all annotators**, not from each annotator's own rates, and it does not require the same annotators to have labelled every item (it does assume every item received the same number of judgements). Krippendorff's alpha [@krippendorff2018content] takes the idea further, writing agreement as $\alpha = 1 - D_o/D_e$ — observed disagreement over expected disagreement — with a distance function you choose, so one coefficient covers nominal, ordinal and interval labels and tolerates missing judgements. The interpretation, and the skew problem, are unchanged for all three.

That difference between "each annotator's own rates" and "one pooled rate" is not bookkeeping; it is the second of the two known situations that affect how kappa is read, and this corpus illustrates it. See below.
:::

### The same reference and lexicon rule, a different sample {#the-same-annotators-a-different-number}

To see the effect of the class ratio, take all 632 reviews A calls negative and a random 632 of the reviews A calls positive. This 1,264-row **artificially balanced subsample** does not estimate agreement on the full test distribution; it shows how the same A and B behave on differently selected texts.

```text
### the identical annotators, on a class-balanced subsample

                    full test set (n=10,000)   balanced (n=1,264)
raw agreement                       93.42%              60.28%
p_e                                 90.99%              50.00%
Cohen's kappa                        0.2698              0.2057
Krippendorff's alpha                 0.2655              0.0722
```

On this subsample raw agreement falls from 93.42% to 60.28%. The decision rules of A and B are the same; the texts evaluated and the class mix are different. The result shows that raw agreement is not a fixed property of the annotators but a measure that changes with the sample.

The two chance-corrected coefficients also part company on the right-hand column, and that gap is the second half of the story. On the full set they agree (0.2698 against 0.2655); on the balanced subsample kappa is nearly three times alpha (0.2057 against 0.0722), from the same data. The mechanism is the one named in the $p_e$ callout above: Cohen's kappa computes $p_e$ from **each annotator's own marginals**, while alpha and Scott's pi use a **single pooled marginal**. On the balanced subsample A is 50% negative by construction and B is roughly 12% — a large divergence in how often the two of them reach for the minority label. Divergent marginals *lower* Cohen's chance baseline (here to 0.50, against 0.57 for the pooled marginal), so the same observed agreement counts as further above chance; alpha's pooled baseline is not lowered by the divergence, so it does not give that credit.

This table illustrates two known situations that affect how kappa is read [@feinstein1990high; @cicchetti1990high]. On the full set a high raw agreement comes with a low kappa (the prevalence effect); on the balanced subsample the different marginals of A and B widen the gap between kappa and alpha (the bias effect). These are not malfunctions of the coefficient; they are examples of the coefficients using different null models and being sensitive to the composition of the sample. Report kappa and alpha together with the marginals and the sampling design.

::: {.column-margin}
One number in that table is exact rather than measured, and the reason is worth a line. On the balanced subsample $p_e = 0.5000$ exactly, because when one annotator is a perfect 50/50 split the expected agreement is $0.5b + 0.5(1-b) = 0.5$ *whatever* the other annotator's rate $b$ is. The coefficient's denominator, $1 - p_e = 0.5$, stops depending on B entirely.
:::

Choosing the coefficient after looking at the table can shift the interpretation. The five summaries of the same 2×2 table below answer different questions; so settle which coefficient you will use, and why, before you look at the results:

```text
### the identical 10,000-row table, five coefficients
raw agreement  p_o                    0.9342
Gwet's AC1                            0.9277
PABAK  (2*p_o - 1)                    0.8684
Cohen's kappa                         0.2698
Krippendorff's alpha                  0.2655
```

Not one of these is wrong. They differ because they make different assumptions about what "chance" means when one class dominates: kappa and alpha assume annotators guess at their observed rates and charge you for the skew; PABAK and AC1 assume they do not, and refuse to [@gwet2008computing]. Which is right depends on which null you think is the fair comparison for your task, not on diagnosing from the table whether anybody guessed. The coefficients differ in what they assume chance agreement *would* look like; none of them can tell you what the annotators were doing. [The five summaries of this table range from 0.27 to 0.93.]{.hl} A good report gives the confusion table, class-specific agreement and a coefficient justified in advance, together.

There is a second lesson hiding in B's scores. Annotator B achieves **93.42% accuracy** against gold. @sec-bake-off's majority-class baseline — label everything positive, read nothing — achieves **93.68%**. B's hand-built lexicon, 73 phrases of careful Turkish, performs *worse than a constant*. On macro-F1 the picture is different (63.27 for B against 48.37 for the constant), which is the whole reason @sec-bake-off refused to report accuracy alone.

There is a third number worth reporting. For one class, **specific agreement** is twice the number of examples on which both chose that class, divided by the total number of times A and B chose it: $2 n_{kk} / (n_{k\cdot} + n_{\cdot k})$. In this binary table the calculation is numerically identical to B's class F1 against A: 96.55% on positive and **30.00%** on negative. The equality comes from the definition of the metric; it does not imply that B is a human or that A is free of error. Specific agreement does what no single chance-corrected number can: it shows where the divergence is. These two label sequences overlap almost completely on praise and very little on complaint.

::: {.anlp-widget}

```{=html}
<div class="widget-title">What agreement is worth at a given prevalence</div>
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof prevalence = Inputs.range([0.02, 0.5], {step: 0.01, value: 0.063, label: "minority class share"})
viewof rawAgreement = Inputs.range([0.5, 1.0], {step: 0.005, value: 0.934, label: "raw agreement"})
viewof bias = Inputs.range([0.0, 1.0], {step: 0.05, value: 0.5, label: "B's minority rate ÷ A's"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
kappaOf = function (prev, obs, ratio) {
  const a = prev;
  const b = Math.min(0.999, Math.max(0.001, prev * ratio));
  // Not every (a, b, p_o) triple comes from a real 2x2 table. With minority
  // rates a and b, observed agreement is confined to |1-a-b| <= p_o <= 1-|a-b|.
  const lo = Math.abs(1 - a - b);
  const hi = 1 - Math.abs(a - b);
  const feasible = obs >= lo - 1e-9 && obs <= hi + 1e-9;
  const pe = a * b + (1 - a) * (1 - b);
  return {pe: pe, lo: lo, hi: hi, feasible: feasible,
          kappa: (!feasible || pe >= 0.9999) ? null : (obs - pe) / (1 - pe)};
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
kappaTable = kappaOf(prevalence, rawAgreement, bias)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<table style="width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;font-size:0.9em">
<tr><td style="padding:4px 8px">observed agreement <i>p<sub>o</sub></i></td>
    <td style="padding:4px 8px;text-align:right;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">${(rawAgreement * 100).toFixed(2)}%</td></tr>
<tr><td style="padding:4px 8px">chance agreement <i>p<sub>e</sub></i></td>
    <td style="padding:4px 8px;text-align:right;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums">${(kappaTable.pe * 100).toFixed(2)}%</td></tr>
<tr><td style="padding:4px 8px;border-top:1px solid #ddd"><b>Cohen's kappa</b></td>
    <td style="padding:4px 8px;text-align:right;border-top:1px solid #ddd;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums"><b>${kappaTable.feasible ? kappaTable.kappa.toFixed(4) : "—"}</b></td></tr>
<tr><td style="padding:4px 8px" colspan="2">${
  !kappaTable.feasible
    ? `these marginals cannot produce this agreement rate — with these rates, p&#8338; must lie between ${(kappaTable.lo * 100).toFixed(1)}% and ${(kappaTable.hi * 100).toFixed(1)}%`
    : kappaTable.kappa < 0 ? "worse than chance" : kappaTable.kappa < 0.2 ? "slight" : kappaTable.kappa < 0.4 ? "fair" : kappaTable.kappa < 0.6 ? "moderate" : kappaTable.kappa < 0.8 ? "substantial" : "almost perfect"}</td></tr>
</table>`
```

The sliders change raw agreement, A's minority rate and the ratio of B's rate to A's *hypothetically*. The same 93.4% agreement is worth kappa ≈ 0.27 at the rates of this table; it would be worth less at more skewed rates and more at balanced ones. Not every setting of the three sliders describes a 2×2 table that can exist; the curve is drawn only over the range where the three choices form a possible table, which is why it covers a short arc rather than the whole axis. The hollow circle marks the measured point of this chapter's table; the other points of the curve are not new experimental results.

The verbal labels under the number — *slight*, *fair*, *moderate*, *substantial*, *almost perfect* — are @landis1977measurement's benchmark scale, and they are worth naming precisely because everyone uses them and almost nobody says where they come from. The authors proposed the bands as "clearly arbitrary" divisions for discussion, not as measured thresholds. Report the number and the interval; treat the adjective as a label for a conversation, never as a passing grade.

:::

### Adjudication

::: {#gloss-adjudication .column-margin .term-gloss}
**adjudication** — an additional review that examines why judgements
disagree and records either the decision or the remaining uncertainty. Some
disagreements improve the guideline; others show a lasting difference of
interpretation. [↩](#term-adjudication){.term-back}
:::

Agreement measurement is diagnostic; [adjudication](#gloss-adjudication){#term-adjudication .term-ref} is the step that follows it. A loop you can follow:

1. **Two annotators label the same 200 items independently of each other.** Not a sample of each — the same items. To be able to see minority cases you can stratify the pilot toward the minority class: at this corpus's 6.3% minority share a plain random 200 contains about thirteen minority items, and most of kappa's numerator comes from those cells. The kappa of such a pilot belongs to the class ratio you chose. If you want to report agreement on the natural distribution, use a separate, representative sample, or state the sampling design explicitly.
2. **Compute the confusion table and an uncertainty interval for kappa together.** The interval is not optional at this size. A kappa's standard error depends on the marginals as well as the sample size, so instead of a ready-made formula use a bootstrap that, as below, resamples the two judgements of the same item together. Resampling this chapter's reference-versus-lexicon table gives a standard error of about 0.02 at 10,000 items and about 0.14 for a plain random 200, which puts the 95% interval around a point estimate of 0.27 at roughly $[-0.02, 0.54]$. On a stratified pilot of 100 gold-negative plus 100 gold-positive items the standard error drops to about 0.04, and the point estimate moves to around 0.21 (kappa depends on the sample's class mix). These numbers belong to the reference-versus-lexicon table; in your own pilot with two humans, compute the interval separately. Fix the target coefficient and the composition of the sample *before* you look at the results, and end the pilot loop (steps 3–5) when the *lower* bound of the interval clears the target; an interval that contains the target is not evidence in either direction. Nor does clearing a threshold show by itself that the schema measures the target correctly.

```python
    from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    idx = (rng.integers(0, len(a), len(a)) for _ in range(2000))
    boot = [cohen_kappa_score(a[i], b[i]) for i in idx]
    lo, hi = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5])
    ```

3. **Read every disagreement together.** Not to decide who was right, but to find out *why* they differed. Disagreements often cluster into a few recurring situations.
4. **Add each situation to the guideline as a decided case with examples on both sides.** This is the deliverable.
5. **Annotate a fresh 200 independently and re-measure.** If agreement did not rise, examine the disagreements again: the cause may be a gap in the guideline, the guideline being applied differently, a change in the sample, or a limit of the schema.

Do not treat step 3 as a vote. Resolving disagreements one by one improves the pilot data. Adding the recurring *kinds of disagreement* to the guideline can also pay off in the next round of annotation; measure its effect on new, independent items.

### What to do with three annotators instead of two

Sending every item to a third person is expensive at scale. So most projects combine a majority decision, a reliability model and expert adjudication of selected disagreements. The diagram at the top of this chapter also named *collapse* — the record of disagreement not being kept when the judgements are merged into one label — as a problem of its own, without saying what to do about it. With a crowd you have several judgements per item; how you reduce them to one label is a choice, and keeping the raw judgements lets you change that choice later.

**Majority vote** is a simple starting method. If the annotators' error rates differ markedly, or their errors depend on one another, weighting the votes equally can lose information. **Latent-variable aggregation** [@dawid1979maximum] estimates each annotator's error pattern (confusion matrix) and the hidden class with a joint probability model, by EM (expectation–maximisation: guess the true labels, re-estimate each annotator's error rates from the guesses, re-guess, and repeat until nothing changes); reference labels are not required. The result depends on the annotators' judgements overlapping enough and on the model's assumptions. Snorkel-style weak supervision also models the reliability of its sources; there the dependence between the labelling functions and the model family have to be specified separately. A third option is to keep the **vote distribution** without reducing it to one label at all, and to train against a soft target: an item two of three annotators called positive gets a positive vote share of 2/3 as its target instead of a hard 1. That number is not, by itself, a calibrated estimate of the probability that the item really is positive; whether the disagreement has to do with the task has to be read separately. In this chapter half of the 40 test reviews the model disputed most strongly were classified as texts that fit a single binary label poorly; on such items a 2–1 split can carry information that a hard label deletes [@uma2021learning; @plank2022problem].

## Auditing labels at scale {#sec-audit}

Reading all 40,000 rows by hand is expensive for most projects. What you can do is set up a procedure that chooses which rows to read first.

Here we use out-of-fold prediction to produce a **review priority**. It is a simple threshold rule inspired by confident learning [@northcutt2021confident], which uses the model's own confidence to find candidate label errors; it is not the method itself. The full method does not use a single global threshold: it thresholds each class at the average probability the model assigns to that class over the examples labelled with it, and builds a count matrix (the *confident joint*) from those thresholds. The single 0.90 threshold below is a shortcut, and per-class thresholds exist to correct exactly this when classes are so imbalanced. Fit on four folds, predict the fifth, repeat. Every training row now has a prediction from a model that never saw that row's label. Rows where the model gives a high score to the *other* class are not automatic verdicts of error; they are candidates to be read by hand.

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold

skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
# Xtr here comes from a vectoriser fitted on all 40,000 rows, before the folds.
# For a fully out-of-fold prediction, fit the vectoriser inside each training fold too.
oof = np.zeros(len(y))
for train_idx, val_idx in skf.split(Xtr, y):
    oof[val_idx] = clf().fit(Xtr[train_idx], y[train_idx]).predict_proba(Xtr[val_idx])[:, 1]

# the score the model gives to the opposite class; not the probability that the label is wrong
wrong_conf = np.where(y == 1, 1 - oof, oof)
```

On the 40,000 training rows:

| threshold | rows flagged | share | gold positive | gold negative |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| > 0.50 | 3,026 | 7.57% | 2,232 | 794 |
| > 0.90 | 92 | 0.23% | 49 | 43 |
| > 0.95 | 34 | 0.09% | 18 | 16 |
| > 0.99 | 2 | 0.005% | 2 | 0 |

: Rows whose opposite-class score exceeds the threshold, to be read by hand {tbl-colwidths="[18,18,14,25,25]"}

We measured what the comment in the code implies. With the vectoriser also fitted on the training part of each fold only, the number of rows above the 0.90 threshold rises from 92 to 123, and at 0.95 from 34 to 47; 89 of the first 92 candidates are in the new list too. The numbers below, and the repair experiment, belong to the first list of 92. In your own audit, fit the vectoriser inside the fold; a `Pipeline` does that by itself.

Three things are worth noticing.

**The flags are class-balanced, the corpus is not.** At the 0.90 threshold, 43 of 92 flags are on gold-negative rows — 47% — in a corpus that is 6.3% negative. Per row, 1.70% of negative labels are flagged against 0.13% of positive ones — the flag rate of a negative label is *thirteen times* higher. That is where to start reading. But it is a difference in flag rates, not error rates: the model may simply be less certain, or worse calibrated, on the minority class.

**The high threshold flags very few rows.** 92 of the 40,000 training rows exceed the 0.90 threshold. The random 100 test rows showed zero outright errors; if the prior-dependent scenario of about 1% from there were right you would expect around 400 errors, but that value is not a measured error rate and cannot be used here as a count of real errors. The rule also leaves out the errors the model cannot detect: it is blind to errors on texts the model itself finds hard. Rows that are not flagged cannot be declared clean.

**A flag is a request to read, not a verdict.** The 92 candidates above are in the training set. In a separate audit I read, as a single person, the 40 reviews of the *test* set on which the model disputed the stored label with the highest score (in the test set a wrong label costs you a wrong leaderboard rather than a slightly lower-scoring model). The two selections have different sampling frames; the proportions of one cannot be carried over to the other. I classified each review by hand into one of three categories: `error` (the gold label clearly contradicts the text), `schema` (a single binary label cannot represent the text), or `model` (the label is defensible and the classifier is wrong).

```text
### 40 highest-confidence gold/model disagreements, test set, read by hand

error   (gold label is wrong)                        11    27.5%
schema  (binary label cannot represent the text)     20    50.0%
model   (label defensible, classifier wrong)          9    22.5%
                                                     --
data-side problems                                   31 / 40

schema breakdown:  mixed 12 · truncated 4 · lukewarm 3 · no verdict 1
```

**Of the 40 selected candidates, 31 show a problem on the data side according to the single reader**: 20 were classified as schema and 11 as a clear label contradiction. These proportions describe only the test examples the model selected with its highest scores; they are not an estimate of a rate for the corpus or for the 92 training candidates. With $n = 40$ the 95% Wilson interval (a confidence interval for a proportion that stays sensible at small $n$) on the schema share runs from about 35% to 65%, and on the error share from 16% to 43%, and the two intervals overlap; but these intervals describe counting uncertainty only and do not correct for purposive selection. The reading was done by a single unblinded reader (me, who had written the hypothesis). The same forty items should be read by a second, blinded reader and the agreement reported; that step tests the subjective classification, and does not by itself solve the problem of generalising. I did not do that, and you should before you quote the number.

Four of the forty show what the categories mean:

- **Row 6874** (gold = negative, model p(positive) = 0.984). Clear praise, no visible reservation; it plainly contradicts the negative label. At which stage the error arose is not known.
- **Row 8356** (gold = positive, p = 0.059). *"yastıklar ince yeterli değil"* — "the pillows are thin, not enough." Labelled positive; another clear contradiction.
- **Row 8006** (gold = positive, p = 0.034). *"hiç bir sebeb göstermeden iade kurallarına uyarak beğenmedim dedim, iade ettim.ücret iadem anında yapıldı.kargo ücreti de dahi."* — "without giving any reason, following the return rules, I said I did not like it and returned it. my refund was made at once. the shipping fee too." The review praises the returns process; it gives no positive verdict on the product, and it reports "I did not like it" as the stated reason for the return. On this example the largest negative contributions to the model's decision score come from the features `iade` ("return", −1.78), `beğenmedim` ("I did not like it", −1.30) and `iade ettim` ("I returned it", −0.65); about half of the negative contributions come from features containing `iade`. Under a "was this a good experience" target the positive label is defensible, which is why we counted this row as a model error. Under the product-targeted guideline v1, the returns process is not the product (case 1): if "I did not like it" counts as a product verdict the label would be 0, and if it does not the row is `SKIP` (case 4). The category depends on the definition of the target, which is one more reason to read the counts as a direction rather than a rate.
- **Row 2544** (gold = positive). *"paketleme başarısız. ampüller fena değil"* — "packaging failed. the bulbs are not bad." Two verdicts of opposite polarity about two different aspects. Which label fits cannot be decided before the target and the rule for mixed reviews are set.

Five of the nine selected model errors involve negation: *fena değil* ("not bad"), *özelliklerinin altında bir ürün değil* ("not a product below its specifications"), and one triple negation. A model that uses word unigrams and bigrams can learn frequent patterns such as *fena değil* as a separate feature; but it does not structurally represent the *scope* of a long or nested negation. That is what happened in this model: on row 2544 the contribution of the bigram `fena değil` to the decision score is only −0.06, while the unigrams `değil` (−1.77) and `fena` (−0.55) dominate. These examples show the limit of this feature setup, not that every n-gram model will get every negation wrong. Models that represent word order and scope are the subject of later chapters (@sec-transformers).

### What cleaning actually bought

Given 92 suspect rows, the obvious next move is to remove them or flip them and retrain. We compared both conditions on the same test split used for reporting throughout the chapter. This is an exploratory comparison; it should not be read as a final result on a never-seen test set:

```text
### repairs, judged on the test split used throughout the chapter

                          acc    macro-F1   F1(neg)
baseline (no repair)     92.57      76.21     56.47
drop 92  (p > 0.90)      92.37      75.72     55.61
flip 92  (p > 0.90)      92.47      75.94     55.99
drop 34  (p > 0.95)      92.39      75.83     55.83
flip 34  (p > 0.95)      92.52      76.03     56.15
drop  2  (p > 0.99)      92.54      76.15     56.37
flip  2  (p > 0.99)      92.52      76.11     56.31
```

**None of these six repair conditions beat the baseline on the test split used.** The largest difference is about half a macro-F1 point (dropping the 92 rows: −0.49). These are the differences observed for the fixed sets of rows that were tried; they are not a confidence interval for the benefit of the method, nor an upper bound that rules out a large gain. Nor does the seed deviation of other experiments stand in for the uncertainty of these deterministic repairs. The right comparison is to apply the same operation to the same number of *random* rows, and we ran that too: 92 random rows with the same class mix as the 92 flags, 20 separate draws.

```text
### control: 92 random rows with the class mix of the flags (49 pos / 43 neg), 20 draws
                            macro-F1     sd      min      max
drop 92 random rows  (mean)    76.15   0.13    75.91    76.45
flip 92 random rows  (mean)    75.87   0.36    75.01    76.47
drop the 92 flagged rows       75.72
flip the 92 flagged rows       75.94
```

Dropping the 92 flagged rows (75.72) is below even the lowest of the 20 draws of dropping 92 random rows (75.91): on this test split, dropping the flagged rows loses more than dropping random rows. Flipping the labels of the flagged rows (75.94) cannot be distinguished from the mean of flipping 92 random labels (75.87). So the rows selected by the model's disagreement do behave differently from random rows, but not in the expected direction of raising the score.

This result shows that producing a review list and raising the score by dropping or flipping the rows on that list wholesale are separate goals. No gain was observed here on the second goal. Two notes:

1. **92 rows out of 40,000 is 0.23% of the training data.** Editing that few rows is not expected to move a model trained on 40,000 examples by much: in the control, dropping 92 random rows moves the score by 0.06 points on average. That the flagged rows move it more (0.49 points) shows that rows near the decision boundary can matter more than their count suggests.
2. **The flagged rows may not all be of one kind.** Of the 40 selected disputes in the test set, 20 were schema problems according to the single reader; for the 92 training candidates that proportion is unknown, and those rows were not read separately. Flipping (which keeps the row) edged out dropping (which removes it) at the 92- and 34-row thresholds, and the order reversed at 2 rows; such small differences are not evidence about why keeping the rows would be better. Read the rows before either operation.

The concrete return of this audit is not the retrained model; it is that schema problems became visible **in the 40 selected disputes**. That gives a reason to re-examine the guideline; it does not show that half of the confusion in the whole corpus comes from the schema. The automated tool finds the candidates; it is the human reading them who revisits the definition of the target. In separate work, @northcutt2021pervasive found label errors in the test sets of ten of the most-used ML benchmarks and showed that model rankings can change when the test labels are corrected: scored against corrected labels, on ImageNet a ResNet-18 overtakes a ResNet-50 once the originally mislabelled examples make up just 6% more of the test set. No such change of ranking was measured in this chapter.

## What label noise costs, and in which direction

Suppose your annotation process has an error rate. How much does it cost? The effect of a label error depends jointly on its direction, on the sizes of the classes and on how many rows change. In the table below the same percentage does not mean the same number of wrong labels in the two directions: the percentages are shares of the source class.

I corrupted the training labels at controlled rates under three regimes, retrained from scratch, and evaluated against the original test labels (no artificial noise added). Three seeds each; standard deviation never exceeded 0.50 macro-F1.

```text
### macro-F1, clean test set, model retrained at each rate
### rates are the share of the SOURCE class flipped; "symmetric" flips that share of EACH class

flip rate      0%     1%     2%     5%    10%    20%    30%    40%
symmetric   76.21  74.18  72.43  68.58  63.34  55.43  49.86  43.71
neg -> pos  76.21  76.14  76.29  76.27  76.42  76.85  77.12  76.47
pos -> neg  76.21  74.17  72.87  68.63  63.63  56.69  52.01  47.99
```

The middle row barely moves: with this model and this class ratio, the macro-F1 of the condition in which **40% of the negative labels are flipped to positive** stays close to the baseline; at 30% it is 0.91 above it. We looked at where the rise comes from: in the 30% condition the model calls fewer reviews negative (about 845 instead of 1,075); precision on the negative class rises from 44.8% to about 50%, and recall falls from 76.3% to 67%. So as negative training labels get scarcer the decision boundary shifts, and on this test split macro-F1 rises a little. That is not a recommendation to corrupt labels. Mind what the percentages mean, too: 40% of the negative class is about 1,000 rows, 40% of the positive class about 15,000. The bottom row loses 28 points over the same range.
