::: {.fig-cap}
Three noise regimes on the same 40,000 training rows, evaluated on the same test split; each condition repeated with three seeds. The percentages are shares of the source class, and the two one-directional curves flip different numbers of rows. The 93.7/6.3 [class imbalance](#gloss-class-imbalance){#term-class-imbalance .term-ref} is an important factor in this asymmetry, not its only explanation.
:::

::::

::: {#gloss-class-imbalance .column-margin .term-gloss}
**class imbalance** — one label is far more common than the other. Here
93.7% of reviews are positive, so a model that answers "positive" every
time looks accurate while finding nothing. [↩](#term-class-imbalance){.term-back}
:::

First the counts on this dataset. The same source-class percentage changes very different numbers of labels when the classes are imbalanced; the effect on the score has to be measured separately on other tasks.

**neg → pos at 10%:** 253 of 2,529 negatives are relabelled positive. The positive class grows to 37,724, of which 253 are wrong — **0.67% contamination**. The negative class shrinks to 2,276 but every remaining member is correct. A smaller, pure minority class is still learnable.

**pos → neg at 10%:** 3,747 of 37,471 positives are relabelled negative. The negative class is now 2,529 correct plus 3,747 wrong — **59.7% mislabelled**. The model is fitting a class whose majority membership is noise. The true negatives still form a coherent cluster, so the model still learns something (63.63, against 48.37 for the majority baseline), but the signal is diluted in the noise, at a cost of 12.58 points.

The same asymmetry appears at rates far too small to notice in a spreadsheet. At **1% pos → neg**, only 375 rows flip — one percent of the *positive class*, which is 0.94% of all training rows, a rate most teams would call excellent. But those 375 rows are **12.9% of everything now labelled negative** (375 of 2,904, the 2,529 real negatives plus the 375 arrivals), and they cost 2.04 macro-F1 points — more than the entire gap between bag of words and tf-idf unigrams in @sec-bake-off, which was 1.56.

Because the percentages mean different numbers of rows in the two directions, we also ran the comparison with the *same number* of labels:

```text
### the same NUMBER of flipped training labels in each direction (3 seeds, mean macro-F1)
    250 labels  neg->pos 76.35 (sd 0.17)   pos->neg 74.98 (sd 0.25)   | share of source class: neg 9.9%  pos 0.67%
    500 labels  neg->pos 76.80 (sd 0.20)   pos->neg 73.64 (sd 0.20)   | share of source class: neg 19.8%  pos 1.33%
   1000 labels  neg->pos 76.95 (sd 0.68)   pos->neg 71.11 (sd 0.27)   | share of source class: neg 39.5%  pos 2.67%
   2000 labels  neg->pos 68.60 (sd 1.02)   pos->neg 67.91 (sd 0.15)   | share of source class: neg 79.1%  pos 5.34%
```

With the same number of labels flipped, the direction still matters: flipping 1,000 positive labels to negative loses 5.1 points, while flipping 1,000 negative labels to positive does not lower the score. But the asymmetry has a limit: with 79% of the negative class (2,000 labels) flipped, that direction loses 7.6 points too.

Two practical suggestions follow from this experiment, each to be tested separately on your own data:

- **Measure your annotation error rate per class, and say which class the errors come *from*.** An overall 1% is not informative by itself: errors that *turn minority rows into majority ones* barely registered here, while errors that *turn majority rows into minority ones* cost 12.58 points at the same 10% class-conditional rate. Name the source class and the target class every time, and give the number of rows along with the percentage.
- **Do not close uncertainty with a guess.** In this experiment the examples wrongly moved from the majority to the minority were the expensive ones; but it does not follow that an annotator should systematically avoid the minority decision — that raises the number of missed minority cases. Send an uncertain item to `SKIP` and to adjudication; that is what the guideline earlier in this chapter is for. Measure the cost of errors, the class ratio and the target metric separately on your own task: where a missed minority case is the expensive error — screening, safety, fraud — the calculation comes out differently.

::: {.column-margin}
This experiment shows that **rates conditional on the source class** can mislead when the classes are imbalanced. Which direction does more harm in spam, fraud, medical screening or content moderation does not follow from this table: a comparison at a fixed number of errors, the class weights, the metric and the operational cost all have to be reassessed. Theory for learning under class-conditional noise is surveyed in @frenay2014classification.

**In this experiment the label corruptions were chosen independently of the text**: at a fixed rate, without looking at the text. Real errors can depend on properties of the text — they can concentrate on hard items, for example — and the effect of the same nominal rate then differs [@wei2022learning]. The hard reviews the model flagged in the previous section do not show the distribution of verified label errors; they only suggest that such concentration is possible. @frenay2014classification separates noise independent of everything, noise depending only on the class, and noise depending on the instance. This experiment's symmetric regime is an example of the first and its two one-directional regimes of the second; the cost of the third was not tested here. So do not read the curves above as a bound.
:::

## Your test labels change what the measurement means {#your-test-set-is-a-ceiling-not-a-ruler}

The previous experiments changed the *training* labels artificially and measured the result against the original test labels. Now the reverse: the predictions of one fixed model, trained once on the original data, are scored against versions of the test labels that have been flipped in a controlled way. The model never changes; what changes is the labels used for scoring. A "clean" or "original" test label here means the version with no artificial noise added; it does not mean a label that has been independently verified as true.

Note the change of denominator, because the word "noise" is doing different work in the two experiments. In the previous section a "1% flip rate" meant one percent *of the source class*. Here it means one percent *of all test rows*, flipped in whichever direction the row happened to be — at this corpus's balance, about 94 positives and 6 negatives per hundred flips. Uniform flipping is a controlled stress test, not a claim about how test labels actually go wrong — the margin note on instance-dependent noise at the end of the previous section applies here too, and real test errors concentrate on the hard rows.

```text
### one fixed model, corrupted test labels, mean of 5 seeds

test noise      acc   macro-F1   F1(neg)   sd(macro-F1)
### noise here = share of ALL test rows, flipped uniformly at random
    0%        92.57      76.21     56.47          0.00
    1%        91.73      74.68     53.90          0.23
    2%        90.85      73.13     51.31          0.12
    5%        88.31      69.41     45.36          0.17
   10%        84.19      64.79     38.66          0.24
   20%        75.48      57.00     28.82          0.36
```

Line these up against chapter 4's leaderboard (@sec-bake-off), which was computed on the original labels:

| system | macro-F1 |
|:---|---:|
| tf-idf 1–2 gram, original test labels | 76.21 |
| tf-idf 1–2 gram, **1%** test-label noise | 74.68 |
| bag of words, original test labels | 73.51 |
| tf-idf 1–2 gram, **2%** test-label noise | 73.13 |
| tf-idf unigram, original test labels | 71.95 |
| tf-idf char\_wb 3–5, original test labels | 70.39 |

: Scores against different label versions of the same test split; the rows cannot be ranked on one common scale {tbl-colwidths="[62,38]"}

**Two percent artificial noise in the test labels takes the same model's macro-F1 from 76.21 down to 73.13.** That number is below the 73.51 bag-of-words scored on the original labels. The model did not get worse: it is byte-for-byte the same model, making byte-for-byte the same predictions. Because the two models are not compared on a common version of the labels, do not conclude that the ranking has reversed: 73.13 is one model measured against noisy labels, 73.51 the other model measured against the original ones.

Would the ranking survive on a *common* noisy version of the labels? In expectation, for independent symmetric flips at rate $\eta < 0.5$, it does: a classifier's noisy accuracy is $\eta + (1 - 2\eta)\,a_{\text{clean}}$, which is increasing in $a_{\text{clean}}$, so the order is preserved on average. On one realised test set it need not be. Take 100 items where A is wrong only on item 3 and B only on items 1 and 2 — on the original labels A scores 99 and B 98. Flip the labels of items 1 and 2 and score both against *those* labels: A drops to 97 and B rises to 100. We measured it for this chapter's pair: scoring bigram TF-IDF and bag-of-words 200 times against the same noisy test labels, the 2.69-point gap between them shrinks to 2.50 on average at 2% noise and to 1.36 at 20%, and the order reverses in none of the 200 draws. That result holds for uniform, independent flips; not for real errors concentrated on hard rows.

What the table shows is that **scores reported against different versions of the labels cannot be compared directly**: the difference between a 73.13 measured on a test set with 2% label noise and someone else's 73.51 measured on the original labels is neither a ranking of models nor evidence that they are statistically indistinguishable. When comparing across studies, report the evaluation set, the definition of the labels and the uncertainty calculation together; "which test set, with which labels" belongs in every comparison.

These comparisons have three consequences for evaluation design:

**The test labels determine how the score is read.** In a hypothetical setup where each true label is flipped independently with probability 2%, the *expected accuracy* of a model that is perfect against the truth is 98% against the noisy labels. That is not a hard upper bound for a single run, nor a ceiling on macro-F1: a model that has learned to reproduce the errors your annotators made can report a higher score. Once your model's error rate approaches your labels', a high score does not by itself show closeness to the real target, and further improvements can become invisible.

**Small differences on a noisy benchmark are not results until you have read the rows the two models disagree on.** Get the reasoning right. The 1.53 points above are a systematic shift of *one model's* score from the clean ruler to a 1%-noisy one (seed standard deviation only 0.23). Compare two models on the *same* test set and that shift applies to both: under independent symmetric noise the expected accuracy gap shrinks only by the factor $(1-2\eta)$, i.e. to 0.98 of itself at 1% noise; for macro-F1 the relation is not linear, but the shift still moves the level, not the gap. What makes a small gap fragile is how many label errors sit on the rows where the two models *disagree* — and real label errors can cluster on the hard rows where models disagree. On this chapter's test set, changing the label of one row moves one model's macro-F1 by 0.02–0.045 points. The effect on the gap between two models depends on which rows they disagree on and on their predictions; there is no fixed threshold. We measured the worst case: to erase chapter 4's 1.2-point gap (tuned TF-IDF 74.71, raw counts 73.51), changing the 18 most damaging labels among the 231 rows the two models disagree on is enough; for the 2.69-point gap between bigram TF-IDF and bag-of-words the number is 41. Those are extreme cases in which the errors fall in the worst places; with randomly scattered errors the gap survives, as shown above. Read the disagreement rows, blind if you can, fix their label errors, and test the gap on a common version of the labels with a paired bootstrap (McNemar for accuracy). @recht2019imagenet and @beyer2020imagenet document what happens when this is taken seriously on a famous benchmark. The 1.53-point shift itself is chiefly a warning against comparing numbers measured against different versions of the labels.

**Set aside a separate quality budget for the test labels.** Independently examining the rows on which models disagree, and the rows of the minority class, is especially worthwhile. Plan quality and sample size for training, validation and the final test from the costs of your own task; a single 10,000/40,000 allocation is not a general rule.

## Leakage: the errors that make you look good {#sec-leakage}

Everything so far has been about labels being *wrong*. This section is about an evaluation risk separate from wrong labels: if information that should not be seen during training, or the test examples themselves, reach the model, the reported score may not represent the intended conditions of use.

::: {#gloss-label-leakage .column-margin .term-gloss}
**label leakage** — target information the model will not have at the time
of use getting into the input, directly or indirectly. The same text sitting
in both training and test is contamination between the splits, which falls
under the wider term **data leakage**. [↩](#term-label-leakage){.term-back}
:::

Label noise and leakage ([label leakage](#gloss-label-leakage){#term-label-leakage .term-ref}) can both stop the reported score from representing performance on the target. Noise does not always lower the score, and leakage does not raise it under every condition; in both cases the direction has to be measured with a controlled comparison.

The raw corpus has 235,165 rows. Exact de-duplication on the text removes 1,657 **extra rows** from them (0.70%). That is not the number of duplicate groups: 1,055 distinct texts occur more than once (2,712 rows in all), and 77 of those groups carry both labels. Chapter 4 did this de-duplication before splitting (@sec-bake-off). Suppose it had not:

```text
### split-before-dedup, the ordinary careless mistake

rows removed by exact de-duplication           1,657   (0.70%)
test rows also present in train                   45   (0.45% of test)
near-duplicates after normalisation               34   (0.34% of test)

same model, same run:
  accuracy on the 45 leaked rows                93.33
  accuracy on the 9,955 clean rows              91.90
  macro-F1 on the leaked rows                   76.76
  macro-F1 on the clean rows                    74.08
```

In this run the 45 test rows that are also in training have a macro-F1 of 76.76, and the other 9,955 rows 74.08. The two subsets differ in their texts and in their class mix — 42 of the 45 rows are positive, and their median length is 2 tokens (19 for the rest) — so the 2.68-point gap cannot be read as the causal gain of memorisation; and at n = 45 macro-F1 is volatile. In 5 of the 45 rows the copy in training carries the other label. Nor can the 74.08 here be compared directly with the 76.21 baseline used elsewhere in the chapter: this run deliberately did *not* de-duplicate before splitting, so it is a different split. The presence of contamination is shown by matching rows; its effect on the score, by a shared evaluation design. A 0.45% contamination is far too little to move the headline number.

To see how the effect changes with the dose, copy a controlled fraction of the test rows into the training data; the vectoriser is refitted on that enlarged training set as well. This is an artificial contamination: it need not produce the same distribution, or the same effect on the score, as natural splitting mistakes.

| test rows copied into train | accuracy | macro-F1 | F1 (negative) |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0% | 92.57 | 76.21 | 56.47 |
| 1% | 92.57 | 76.27 | 56.60 |
| 2% | 92.62 | 76.41 | 56.86 |
| 5% | 92.65 | 76.53 | 57.08 |
| 10% | 92.82 | 77.14 | 58.20 |
| 25% | 93.33 | 78.59 | 60.82 |
| 50% | 94.00 | 80.89 | 65.07 |
| 100% | 95.62 | 85.89 | 74.17 |

: What leakage is worth, at controlled doses {tbl-colwidths="[34,22,22,22]"}

In this controlled copying experiment the 10% condition takes macro-F1 from 76.21 to 77.14, and the 100% condition to 85.89 (9.68 points — more than twice the 4.3 points that moving from unigram to bigram TF-IDF bought in chapter 4). The effect is specific to this model, this dataset and this copying setup; it is not a fixed gain per 10%, nor an estimate of the effect of a natural leak. Which rows are copied moves the result too: re-running the 10% dose with three different draws, macro-F1 ranged from 76.81 to 77.13.

Controlled copying can produce an increase in score that looks plausible: the 10% dose gives a difference of the size you would expect from a genuine modelling improvement, and it cannot be told apart by looking at the score alone. So verify an unexpectedly good result with checks on the split, on duplicates and on preprocessing.

Now the near-duplicates. On the de-duplicated split of chapter 4, normalising away case, punctuation and whitespace finds 34 test rows whose normalised form also appears in training. Their macro-F1 is **67.62** against **76.23** on the rest. On such a small, selected subset the reason for the gap cannot be determined without examining the texts one by one; macro-F1 on thirty-four rows is close to meaningless. In our recount (32 rows, depending on the details of the normalisation) 31 of these rows are positive and their median length is 3 tokens (*"güzel ürün"*, *"tavsiye ederim"*, *"teşekkürler hb"*); so the F1 of the negative class is decided by a single row. Duplicates have a side benefit as well: every duplicate group in which the same text carries different labels is a candidate for review. The possible reasons are a clear error, a different target, missing context or schema ambiguity; the count does not by itself give a label-noise rate (exercise 9).

### The leaks worth checking for

Check these six risks separately, against your own data and your own setup of use:

1. **Exact duplicates across splits.** *Before* splitting, group by the text; if the same text carries different labels, examine that conflict first (77 groups in this corpus). Then de-duplicate by a rule you have documented (`df.drop_duplicates(subset="text")` keeps the first row of each text), or make sure each group stays in a single split.
2. **Near-duplicates.** Normalise case, punctuation and whitespace; then compare. For longer texts, compare the sets of overlapping word n-grams ("shingles") with Jaccard similarity — shared shingles divided by all shingles — or with MinHash, a fast approximation of it that scales to millions of documents.
3. **Group leakage.** Multiple reviews by the same user, multiple sentences from the same document, multiple images of the same patient. If your target use requires it, split on the *group*, not the row; because the rows genuinely differ, this leak is easy to miss. This corpus has no reviewer identifiers (see the datasheet below), so user-level groups cannot be verified directly; report that limitation.
4. **Temporal leakage.** If your model will run on future data, your test set must be from the future. A random split lets the model see next month while predicting last month.
5. **Preprocessing leakage.** Fit the vectoriser, the scaler and the feature selector on the relevant training part only; on the test set, only transform (chapter 4's pipeline had `vec.fit_transform(train)` and then `vec.transform(test)`). In cross-validation apply the same rule inside every fold: in this chapter's out-of-fold audit the vectoriser had been fitted before the folds, and fitting it inside the fold raised the candidate list from 92 to 123 (@sec-audit).
6. **Benchmark contamination.** Public test texts may have entered the pretraining data of the pretrained model you are fine-tuning. @kapoor2023leakage catalogue kinds of leakage across 17 scientific fields; @magar2022data measure, with controlled pretraining, the effect of contamination on scores; @oren2024proving propose a statistical test of whether a specific dataset is in a black-box model's pretraining data. Report the assumptions and error probabilities of such a test; do not read its result as a definitive provenance record for individual texts. In LLM evaluation this becomes the central problem (@sec-llm-eval).

## Where to spend the next thousand labels

On a fixed annotation budget you choose between the number of examples and the cost of producing and checking each label: careful labels cost more, so you get fewer. This section examines the effect of that choice on the score by varying the number of labels and the level of artificial noise for the same model.

Before the grid, one paragraph on what "cost more" means, because there is a person on the other end of it. A cost example: at a labelling speed of 200 short reviews an hour, 40,000 labels take about 200 person-hours. The real speed depends on the guideline, the length of the texts, breaks and adjudication; measure it in a small pilot before planning. Three points follow, and they are engineering matters and not only ethical ones. **Pay and time targets set the working conditions** and can affect an annotator's attention. This chapter did not measure the effect of piece-rate versus hourly pay on quality; plan fair pay, rest, a clear guideline, a reasonable number of control items (questions with known answers, attention checks, monitoring of agreement between annotators) and a route for appeal and adjudication together. **Task design is a working condition**: a `SKIP` option and decided examples can keep an annotator from being forced into a binary decision on an ambiguous case; measure the effect on speed, fatigue and agreement in the pilot. And on some tasks — moderation, safety, abuse detection — **exposure is a real cost**, and a project that budgets annotator hours without budgeting rotation and support is under-costed [@gray2019ghost; @sambasivan2021everyone]. Record in your datasheet who labelled, how they were paid and at what rate, stating the unknowns explicitly as well; @gebru2021datasheets asks for this.

The grid below trains the same model at seven budget sizes and six noise levels, three seeds each, and evaluates all 42 cells against the same original test labels. In each cell the training rows are drawn at random, the vectoriser is fitted on those rows only, and the labels of each class are flipped at the same rate. (In chapter 4's learning curve the vectoriser had been fitted on all 40,000 reviews, so the two curves cannot be compared directly — there bigram TF-IDF averaged 51.7 at 1,000 labels.)

```text
### macro-F1 by budget and label noise (clean test set, 3 seeds)

                 0%      5%     10%     20%     30%     40%
    500       59.44   58.56   55.57   51.18   47.40   42.12
  1,000       63.71   60.91   57.77   52.32   46.99   42.78
  2,500       68.76   64.17   60.03   53.36   48.23   42.93
  5,000       71.69   66.00   60.21   53.17   47.86   42.42
 10,000       73.72   66.47   61.81   54.46   48.53   42.88
 20,000       74.89   66.99   62.04   55.21   49.09   43.81
 40,000       76.21   68.18   63.20   55.74   49.34   44.16
```

The grid does not separate the *direction* of the noise: it is a separate experiment for noise that corrupts each class at the same rate. The last row (40,000) is close to the symmetric row of the earlier table (68.18 against 68.58 at 5%, 63.20 against 63.34 at 10%), but it comes from separate runs. Re-running the same cells with ten seeds each gave a standard deviation of about half a point (68.38 ± 0.48 at 5%; 62.66 ± 0.46 at 10%), so these differences are at the level of seed-to-seed variation. If you know the direction of your noise, use the earlier table.

Read across a row and you learn what noise costs. Read down a column and you learn what volume buys. Read diagonally and you get the finding:

- **In this grid 1,000 clean labels scored 63.71 macro-F1 and 40,000 labels at 10% noise 63.20.** The observed difference is 0.51 points and rests on three seeds. We re-ran the two cells with ten seeds each: 1,000 clean labels scored 62.24 (sd 2.24; 59.29–65.44), 40,000 labels at 10% noise 62.66 (sd 0.46). The small clean set is ahead in 37 of the hundred seed pairs. So this pair is a tie, and the score of the small set depends heavily on which 1,000 rows were drawn.
- **500 clean labels (59.44) are ahead of 40,000 labels at 20% noise (55.74).** In the ten-seed re-run the difference is 3.9 points, in the same direction in all hundred seed pairs.
- **What volume buys depends on the label noise.** Going from 500 to 40,000 labels brings **16.77** macro-F1 points at 0% noise and **2.04** at 40%. The grid shows the balance of quality and quantity; assessing the return per unit of money takes the costs of annotation and quality control, which have to be known separately.

### Not all labels are worth the same

The grid assumed labels are drawn at random. They need not be. **Uncertainty sampling**, one of the common methods of active learning [@settles2009active], fits a model on a small seed set and chooses the next labels from the examples that model is least decided about.

```python
# schematic: X_seed, y_seed, X_pool and pool have to be prepared beforehand
m0 = clf().fit(X_seed, y_seed)                       # 200 random labels
unc = np.abs(m0.predict_proba(X_pool)[:, 1] - 0.5)   # distance from 0.5
picks = pool[np.argsort(unc)[:800]]                  # the 800 examples scored closest to 0.5
```

This fragment is not a runnable experiment by itself; it summarises the workflow. The lowest `unc` selects the examples whose model score is closest to 0.5; the calibration of the scores was not checked here.

With a budget of exactly 1,000 labels, mean of three seeds:

```text
### 1,000 labels, spent two ways

                              negatives found    acc   macro-F1   F1(neg)
1,000 drawn at random                      62  93.50      65.49     34.40
200 random + 800 uncertain                248  93.59      68.80     40.99
```

The 1,000 examples chosen by uncertainty contain 248 negative labels, the randomly chosen ones 62 — four times as many. That may have improved coverage of the minority class; but the selection also changes how hard the texts are and how close they lie to the decision boundary. How much of the 6.59-point difference in negative-class F1 comes from the number of negative examples cannot be said without a separate comparison.

In these two rows, with the same budget of 1,000 labels, uncertainty sampling scored 68.80 macro-F1 and random selection 65.49: an observed difference of 3.31 points. Because paired differences per seed are not reported, do not generalise it as a definite effect size. Re-running the experiment with a protocol we set up ourselves (the seed model on the vectoriser of the 40,000 texts, the final model on a vectoriser fitted on the 1,000 selected rows), the difference came out at 5.3 and 5.2 points in two groups of three seeds (63.13 → 68.46 and 61.96 → 67.19); the number of negatives found averaged between 188 and 290 depending on the group. The direction is the same; the size is sensitive to the protocol and to the seed.

Putting it next to the budget grid — *1,000 uncertainty-sampled (68.80) matches 2,500 random (68.76)* — is the more quotable claim and the weaker one: the two tables do not share a baseline (random 1,000 is 63.71 in the grid and 65.49 here). That 1.78-point gap is inside the seed-to-seed deviation of the 1,000-label cell (2.24 points over ten seeds); so no separate explanation is needed for two three-seed means differing, but do not treat the 2.5× "discount" as a measurement either.

Keep three limits in view. A training set chosen by uncertainty does not represent the natural test distribution; build the test set with independent, appropriate sampling, and **never** select it this way. How small a seed set is enough depends on the task and the class ratio; 20 and 200 seed labels were not compared here. And the selected set can be **tied to the model that selected it**: a set chosen as uncertain for a linear TF-IDF classifier is not necessarily a good set for the transformer you fine-tune later (@sec-classification-finetune). Such a set has been measured to underperform a random sample of the same size once the architecture changes [@lowell2019practical]; test the transfer to another architecture against random sampling with an equal budget.

## Labels you do not write by hand

Hand annotation is not the only source of labels, and on a 235,000-row corpus it takes a great deal of labour; choose its scope from your budget and your goal. The three methods below can reduce the need for human labels, but they do not by themselves take the place of quality control. Each comes with its own kind of problem.

**Weak supervision.** You write partial, noisy labelling functions and combine them. The lexicon rule in this chapter is one such source. Frameworks like Snorkel [@ratner2017snorkel] fit a generative model over many functions; under the chosen model assumptions it estimates the accuracy of the sources and the dependencies between them from the functions' agreements and conflicts, and it needs no reference labels. The thing to watch is dependence: five variations on the same keyword list should not count as five independent pieces of evidence, and an aggregation model that assumes independence trusts that "consensus" too much. Test the dependence and the coverage of the functions on a small sample with verified labels.

**Distant supervision.** Use an existing signal as a proxy label: star ratings for sentiment, a knowledge base for relation extraction, user clicks for relevance. Cheap and abundant. The risk is that the proxy is not the target — a 3-star review is not "neutral", it is whatever that platform's users mean by three stars, and the mapping shifts across platforms and across years.

**LLM labelling.** You prompt a large model to label your data; @sec-prompting covers the mechanics. On some well-specified tasks, labelling by prompt has matched or beaten non-expert crowdworkers [@gilardi2023chatgpt]; on subjective or culturally loaded tasks the margin shrinks and sometimes reverses [@ziems2024can]. In the cost comparison, count the labour of checking and correcting as well as the model calls. Three things to hold on to. First, LLM labels inherit the model's systematic biases; those do not disappear by collecting more rows, and their size and direction have to be measured on your task. Second, LLM labels may *not be independent* of a model you then evaluate: if the same model family labelled your test set, your evaluation partly measures agreement with that family, and models have been shown to prefer their own output [@panickssery2024llm]. Third, you still need a human-labelled test set to know whether any of it worked: treat LLM labels as an unvalidated instrument and report accuracy and disagreement on a held-out sample that humans have examined independently [@pangakis2023automated]. One more caution for Turkish: the measurements above were made on English data; on user text with misspellings and missing Turkish characters the result may differ (@sec-turkish-nlp), so make this measurement on your own Turkish data.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Synthetic data and the quality filter {#synthetic-data-and-the-quality-filter-that-decides-everything}

Generating training text with an LLM — Self-Instruct [@wang2023selfinstruct] and its descendants — is a common option. Its benefit depends on selection, filtering and comparison with real data as well as on the generation method.

Three kinds of problem are worth knowing by name:

**Lack of diversity.** You can ask for 10,000 negative reviews and get variations on a small number of templates. Examine examples by hand; measures such as the ratio of distinct n-grams and embedding-space coverage (with the tools of chapter 3, @sec-embeddings) are not sufficient by themselves, but they make repetition visible. This is a separate problem from the recursive model collapse below.

**Distributional mismatch.** Generated text is fluent, well-punctuated, and correctly spelled. Real Turkish product reviews are none of those things; @sec-turkish-nlp showed how much of the signal lives in exactly the messiness a generator smooths away. A model trained on clean synthetic text and deployed on real text is being asked to generalise across a shift you introduced yourself.

**Recursive contamination.** Training on the output of models trained on model output degrades over generations — @shumailov2024curse calls it model collapse. The tails of the distribution disappear first, which means the rare cases go first, which means exactly the cases you needed the model for. The condition matters, though, and it is easy to drop: that result *replaces* the real data at each generation. When real data is **accumulated** alongside the synthetic instead of swapped out — which is what actually happens in practice — the test error stays bounded and the collapse largely disappears [@gerstgrasser2024model]. The cautious working rule that follows is narrower than "synthetic data is dangerous": watch the risk of new synthetic generations taking the place of the real data. Using them together with real data, and keeping a fixed, independent evaluation set outside the loop, makes that risk easier to measure [@shumailov2024curse; @gerstgrasser2024model]. Which ratio and which filtering help is something to try on your own task.

For the test set: the main test set should rest on real texts selected independently from the distribution of the target use, and on labels that have been reliably examined. Synthetic examples can be used in additional stress tests; they do not replace the main estimate of performance.
:::

## Write it down: datasheets and model cards

The audits in this chapter produced observations that need documenting: 20.03% of the test reviews contain a contrastive connective; 20 of the 40 test reviews the model disputed with its highest scores are schema problems according to a single reader; in training, the flag rate of negative-labelled rows is thirteen times that of positive ones. Unless you write these observations down, together with how they were sampled and what their limits are, they disappear.

@gebru2021datasheets proposed datasheets for datasets: a standard document covering motivation, composition, collection, preprocessing, uses, distribution, and maintenance. @mitchell2019model proposed model cards, the same idea for trained models, with performance disaggregated across the groups that matter. Both are conventions, not standards, and both are frequently treated as compliance paperwork.

Do not leave the datasheet as a form that merely gets filled in. Tie the provenance of the data, the conditions of use and the known limits to a stage that the decision-makers review before release. @sambasivan2021everyone found, across 53 practitioner interviews, that data problems were pervasive, expensive, and consistently under-valued relative to modelling — "everyone wants to do the model work, not the data work". Actually using the document can reduce that invisibility.

Here is what an honest extract for this chapter's corpus looks like:

```text
### datasheet extract — Turkish product reviews

COMPOSITION
  235,165 reviews; 233,508 after exact de-duplication (1,657 extra rows,
  0.70%). 93.7% positive. 77 texts carry both labels. Product category,
  date, and reviewer are not available.

LICENCE AND PROVENANCE
  The licence file of the original GitHub repository and the licensing
  section of the card say CC BY-SA 4.0; the licence field at the top of
  the Hugging Face page says "unknown" (checked on 10 October 2026).
  The site and the date of collection are not documented.

LABELS
  Provenance unknown; how the labels were derived is not documented
  (possibly from star ratings). No guideline document exists. Whether
  inter-annotator agreement was measured is not reported.

KNOWN LIMITATIONS
  - 20.03% of the test reviews contain one of the connectives ama/fakat/
    ancak/lakin; that alone does not show mixed sentiment or a problem
    with the binary schema. Model macro-F1 on this subset is 72.11,
    against 77.72 on the rest.
  - The 40 test reviews the model disputed with its highest scores were
    examined by one reader: 11 clear label contradictions, 20 schema
    problems. These proportions cannot be generalised to the corpus.
  - In 100 randomly selected test rows the same reader found 0 clear
    contradictions and 7 undecidable rows. The "rule of three" upper
    bound of about 3% for zero observations holds under independent
    sampling and the same definition of an error.
  - Selection bias: reviewers are self-selected. Non-reviewers absent.
    (Not measured.)

RECOMMENDED USE
  Within the terms of the licence, teaching Turkish text classification
  and comparing methods.
NOT RECOMMENDED / NEEDS FURTHER VALIDATION
  Deployments where errors on the negative class (missed or false
  complaints) are costly are not recommended without independent,
  task-specific validation. The highest-scoring model here reaches a
  negative-class F1 of about 56; for an operational decision the
  threshold and the cost of errors have to be assessed separately.
```

Note the shape of it. This draft makes the measured numbers and the undocumented fields visible in one place, and the "not recommended" section is specific enough to stop someone. A good datasheet also records, explicitly, the limitations it cannot put a number on.

## Where the effort actually goes

That is a long list of things that can go wrong. To plan a week of work, use the activities below as an example order. This chapter did not measure their durations or their returns; they are not written into the table, and you have to measure them in your own pilot.

| activity | duration | the information it can give | when to do it |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| read 100 random rows by hand | measure in a pilot | candidates for clear contradictions and ambiguity; a wide uncertainty interval for the rate | when the data arrives, before modelling |
| write a guideline with examples | measure in a pilot | how clear the decision rules are | before bulk annotation |
| measure two humans' agreement on a shared sample | measure in a pilot | a disagreement table and a kappa that depends on the sampling | in the guideline pilot |
| out-of-fold flagging + hand reading | measure in a pilot | candidate rows to examine | once training data exists |
| leakage audit | measure in a pilot | risks in the split and the preprocessing | before reporting a result |

: An example workflow for data-quality activities {tbl-colwidths="[16,29,32,23]"}

[Strengths]{.pro} — reading random rows, writing a guideline and running an agreement pilot can bring out, early, problems that would be invisible later; a leakage audit reduces the risk of publishing a wrong number. Measure their costs and returns on your own task.

[Weaknesses]{.con} — out-of-fold flagging produces a list of candidates and feels like automation. In this chapter, dropping or flipping the list wholesale without examining it did not raise the score; dropping the flagged rows lost more than dropping random rows. Put the labour of review and adjudication into the plan.

## The thing this chapter is really about

Chapter 4 compared representations (@sec-bake-off); this chapter asked what that comparison is measured against. With that chapter's highest-scoring model held fixed and 2% of the test labels flipped artificially, macro-F1 fell from 76.21 to 73.13. That number is below the 73.51 another model scored on the original labels; but the two numbers belong to different versions of the labels. So this experiment does not show a ranking reversing on a shared test set — when we scored the two models against the same noisy labels, the order changed in none of 200 draws. What it shows is the risk of comparing across studies without reporting which version of the labels was used.

The result means that the quality of the evaluation labels has to be reported along with the model's score. The concrete version, in five lines:

- **Read your data.** A hundred rows, by hand, before modelling. Most of the observations in this chapter came from reading rows.
- **Audit the schema too.** Of the 40 model-selected test disagreements examined by a single reader, 20 were counted as schema problems and 11 as clear label contradictions. That is a reason to review the guideline; it is not an estimate of rates in the corpus.
- **Report the source class together with the number of rows affected.** In this experiment, flipping 40% of the negatives to positive kept macro-F1 close to the baseline; flipping 1% of the positives to negative lowered it by 2.04 points. The two percentages correspond to different numbers of rows; the direction also mattered when the same number of labels was flipped, but the result does not carry over directly to other tasks.
- **Test quality and volume together on your own budget.** In this grid 500 clean labels came out ahead of 40,000 labels with 20% artificial noise, while 1,000 clean labels and 40,000 labels at 10% noise could not be told apart. The choice also takes the real cost of labels, the target distribution and the quality of an independent test set.
- **Audit for leakage before you report a result**, especially when the number is unexpectedly good.

These constraints do not relax as the models get larger. @sec-language-models and @sec-transformers introduce systems with orders of magnitude more capacity, and every one of them is trained against labels somebody manufactured and evaluated against a test set somebody could have contaminated. The models change; the problem of the quality of the evaluation labels does not — it only gets harder to see, which is why @sec-llm-eval and @sec-production-eval have to return to it.

## Intuition checks

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Two annotators agree on 93% of items. Is that good?

Unanswerable without the two annotators' marginals. On this corpus, 93.42% agreement gave kappa 0.27, because $p_e$ under an independence null was 90.99%. The same two annotators on a balanced subsample agreed on only 60.28%. Raw agreement is mostly a property of the sample, not the annotators. Always report the confusion table alongside.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Your annotators mislabel 10% of items. How much macro-F1 will you lose?

Depends entirely on direction. Mislabelling 10% of the minority class as majority moved macro-F1 by **+0.21** (76.21 → 76.42) — that is, not at all. Mislabelling 10% of the majority class as minority cost **12.58 points** (76.21 → 63.63). Note what "10%" means in each case: it is the same *class-conditional* rate, not the same overall one. At a 93.7/6.3 split, flipping a tenth of the minority touches 0.63% of the corpus and flipping a tenth of the majority touches 9.37% — fifteen times as many rows. Part of the asymmetry is that, and part of it is that macro-F1 weights the small class equally; the imbalance drives both.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Model A beats model B by 1.2 macro-F1 on your test set. Ship A?

Not yet — but get the reason right. On this corpus 1% test-label noise shifted *one model's* score by 1.53 points. That is a systematic shift that applies to A and B alike on the same test set, so it does not by itself erase a 1.2-point gap (the expected accuracy gap shrinks by only ~2%). What makes the gap fragile is label errors on the rows where the two models *disagree*: on this test set one or two dozen of them are enough to erase 1.2 macro-F1 points, and errors tend to cluster on exactly those hard rows. Read the rows where A and B disagree, fix their label errors, then test the gap with a paired bootstrap.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## An automated audit flags 92 of your 40,000 training labels. Delete them?

No. Read them. When measured, dropping those 92 rows made every metric slightly *worse* (76.21 → 75.72 macro-F1) — a change within seed noise, but certainly not the improvement deletion promises. The likeliest reason is that a large share of them were not errors but cases with mixed or truncated content for which a binary label can be neither right nor wrong — that is what the hand audit found, on a separate sample of 40 flagged rows from the *test* set, so read it as an indication of what the training flags contain rather than a measurement of them. Flipping beat dropping, which fits. The flags are a reading list.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## You have budget for 5,000 careful labels or 40,000 cheap ones. Which?

Careful, unless "cheap" means under roughly 3% error. 5,000 clean labels scored 71.69. The 40,000 scored 76.21 clean, but only 68.18 at 5% noise and 63.20 at 10% — so interpolating, the eight-fold larger set stops being worth it somewhere near 2.8% error. And regardless of the choice, spend the careful budget on the test set first — you cannot measure past your labels' quality.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-data-annotation-interview}

Data quality questions separate candidates faster than modelling questions,
because almost everyone has trained a classifier and almost nobody has audited a
label set. Every answer below is measured in this chapter.

::: {.column-margin}
A tell worth knowing: candidates who have actually shipped a labelled dataset
answer these in terms of *direction* and *which split* — noise into which class,
errors in train or in test. Candidates who have only read about it answer in
terms of a single rate. [The rate is almost never the question.]{.hl}
:::

1. **Your annotators agree 93% of the time. Is the dataset good?** You cannot
   tell, and the reason is chance agreement. Here, 93.42% raw agreement gave
   Cohen's kappa of **0.27**, because with a 93.7/6.3 class split the agreement
   expected under an independence null is already **90.99%** — two annotators
   who both guess the majority label agree almost all the time while conveying
   nothing. The same pair on a balanced subsample agreed on only **60.28%**.
   Say the condition out loud when you quote these numbers: the second
   "annotator" here is a lexicon rule, not a second human, so this is a
   worked demonstration of the arithmetic and not a human agreement study.
   Ask for the confusion table and both annotators' marginals, then compute
   kappa yourself.
   Bonus: say that kappa has its own pathology on skewed data, so report raw
   agreement, kappa *and* the marginals rather than picking whichever flatters.

2. **How much will 10% label noise cost you?** The right first move is to
   refuse the question as posed and ask which direction. Measured on this
   corpus: mislabelling 10% of the minority class as majority moved macro-F1 by
   **+0.21** — nothing. Mislabelling 10% of the majority class as minority cost
   **12.58 points**. [The same *class-conditional* rate, and one direction is
   free while the other is catastrophic]{.hl}, entirely because of the
   imbalance — note that the two are not the same overall corruption: at a
   93.7/6.3 split, a tenth of the minority is 0.63% of the corpus and a tenth
   of the majority is 9.37%. You can corrupt
   **40%** of the negative class into positive and lose nothing measurable.

3. **Where do you spend a limited labelling budget — train or test?** Test,
   disproportionately, and this is the answer most candidates get backwards.
   Training tolerates noise, especially in the majority class. Test tolerates
   none: with 2% test-label noise a perfect classifier scores 98%, and you
   cannot measure past your labels' quality. The number that makes it concrete:
   **2% noise in the test labels drags @sec-bake-off's winner below the score
   its rival earned on clean labels** — same model, same predictions, byte for
   byte, with only the ruler moved. State the condition with it: those are two
   differently labelled test sets, so it is a comparison across conditions and
   not a rank reversal on a shared one.

4. **A new model beats production by 1.2 macro-F1. Ship it?** Not on that
   number alone — but get the reason right. On this corpus 1% test-label
   noise shifted *one model's* score by 1.53 points; on a shared test set that
   systematic shift applies to both models and does not by itself erase the
   gap (the expected accuracy gap shrinks by the factor $(1-2\eta)$, i.e. by only ~2%).
   What makes the gap fragile is label errors on the rows where the two models
   *disagree*: on this test set one or two dozen are enough to erase 1.2
   points. Read the disagreement rows, fix their label errors, and test the gap
   with a paired bootstrap (McNemar for accuracy). @sec-bake-off's 15-point
   gaps survive this easily — [the question is never "is the gap big" but "is
   the gap bigger than the label errors on the rows where the models
   disagree"]{.hl}. The 1.53-point shift is a warning against comparing
   numbers measured on different test sets.

5. **How would you find bad labels in 40,000 rows you cannot read?** Out-of-fold
   prediction, a simplified, single-threshold form of confident learning
   [@northcutt2021confident] (the full method uses per-class thresholds).
   Fit on four folds, predict the fifth; where a model that never saw a row is
   confident in the other class, flag it. Then say the three things the
   measurement taught: only **92 of 40,000** rows flag above 0.90 confidence, so
   it finds far fewer errors than exist; a negative-labelled row is **thirteen
   times** more likely to be flagged, which tells you where to start reading (a
   difference in flag rates, not error rates); and dropping the flagged rows made every metric slightly *worse*
   (76.21 → 75.72, within seed noise — but no gain), which fits an audit — of a separate flagged sample — that
   found about half were texts a binary label can be neither right nor wrong
   about. [A flag is a
   reading list, not a verdict.]{.hl}

6. **How do you check for leakage?** Name the six kinds and the one-line test
   for each: exact duplicates (`drop_duplicates` *before* the split — this
   corpus had 1,657), near-duplicates (normalise case and punctuation, then
   compare), group leakage (split on user or document, not row), temporal
   leakage (test must be from the future), preprocessing leakage (`fit` on train
   only, never on the concatenation), and benchmark contamination
   [@kapoor2023leakage]. Then quantify the stakes: a **10% leak buys about one
   macro-F1 point** — indistinguishable from a real improvement — and a 100%
   leak buys nearly ten. Close with the discipline that catches it: audit the
   numbers you *like*, because leakage only ever makes you look better.

7. **Your annotators disagree constantly. Do you retrain them?** Read the
   disagreements first, because on this corpus **half of the confident
   disagreements were texts a binary label cannot express** — mixed reviews,
   truncated text, reviews about delivery rather than product. That is a schema
   failure, and no amount of annotator training fixes it. Adding a *mixed* or
   *not-applicable* class does. The general form: when agreement is low, the
   question is whether your annotators are unreliable or your label set is
   under-specified, and only reading tells you which.

## Where to go deeper


| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [Data-Centric AI (MIT)](https://dcai.csail.mit.edu/) | a whole course on the premise of this chapter — that improving the data beats improving the model |
| [`cleanlab`](https://github.com/cleanlab/cleanlab) | the label-error detection of @northcutt2021confident as a library; run it on your own training set and read what it flags |
| [`doccano`](https://github.com/doccano/doccano) | a self-hosted annotation tool that takes an afternoon to set up, which removes the usual excuse for annotating in a spreadsheet |
| [`argilla`](https://github.com/argilla-io/argilla) | annotation with disagreement kept rather than averaged away, which is @aroyo2015truth's argument made operational |
| [Eugene Yan's writing](https://eugeneyan.com/writing/) | practical posts on labelling, guidelines and the economics of annotation |

: Beyond the papers {tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}

- @gebru2021datasheets and @mitchell2019model — the two documentation conventions everything else references. Short, readable, and worth copying the section headings from directly.
- @northcutt2021confident for the theory behind out-of-fold flagging, and @northcutt2021pervasive for what it found in ten standard benchmarks — including how little label noise it takes to reorder models scored against corrected test labels.
- @artstein2008inter — the clearest treatment of agreement coefficients for NLP specifically, including when kappa is the wrong tool.
- @aroyo2015truth and @plank2022problem — the argument that annotator disagreement is signal about the task, not noise to be averaged away. This reframes most of what this chapter treats as a problem.
- @sambasivan2021everyone — 53 interviews on why data work is under-valued in practice. Read it before your first industrial project rather than after.
- @kapoor2023leakage for a taxonomy of leakage across 17 scientific fields, and @bender2018data on data statements as a documentation practice with a specific bias focus.
- @klie2023annotation surveys automatic annotation-error detection methods, if you want more than the single out-of-fold technique used here.
- @pustejovsky2012natural is the book-length treatment of running an annotation project — schema design, guideline iteration, adjudication. If this chapter is the argument, that book is the manual.
- @marcus1993penn is worth reading as a historical document: the Penn Treebank guidelines are the reason a generation of NLP agreed on what a parse tree looks like, and they show what "decided cases" look like when taken seriously over years.
- @bowman2021will on why benchmark quality, not model capacity, is increasingly the binding constraint — the natural sequel to this chapter's argument about label noise ceilings.

## Lab: run a small annotation project end to end

Work in pairs. The point is to produce a guideline and an agreement number, not a good model.

1. **Draw 200 items** from the Turkish review corpus with a fixed seed — 100 gold-negative and 100 gold-positive, for the reason given under Adjudication: a plain random 200 would contain about thirteen negatives. Both partners get the identical 200 items, shuffled, and do not see the gold labels.
2. **Write guideline v0 together** — the class definitions only, no decided cases. Ten minutes, no more.
3. **Annotate the first 100 items independently.** Allow `SKIP`. Record how long it took.
4. **Compute raw agreement, Cohen's kappa with a bootstrap interval, and the confusion table.** Report all four. Do *not* compare your number to this chapter's 0.2698 — that one is gold-versus-a-lexicon, not human-versus-human, and they are different quantities. Compare it instead to the kappa reported by two or three published sentiment-annotation studies that used a written guideline, and treat anything much lower as a statement about your guideline rather than about your annotators.
5. **Read every disagreement together** and group them into recurring situations. You should find three to five.
6. **Write guideline v1**, adding each situation as a decided case with a worked example on both sides. Follow the format in this chapter.
7. **Annotate the remaining 100 items** independently under v1 and re-measure. Report the change in kappa and say honestly whether it came from the guideline or from practice.
8. **Compare to the provided gold labels.** For every item where you and your partner agreed but gold disagreed, decide which is right. Report how many gold labels you believe are wrong, and how many are texts your schema cannot express — the same two categories used in @sec-audit.

Deliverable: guideline v1, the two confusion tables, both kappa values, and a one-paragraph statement of what your schema cannot represent.

## Exercises

1. Take a public dataset you might use and answer the six questions in this chapter: who produced the text, who produced the labels, what question they were answering, what licence applies, what consent existed, and what is missing. Write down which you cannot answer — the gaps are the result.
2. Two annotators label 100 items and agree on 90. Compute Cohen's kappa when *both* annotators use the positive label 50% of the time, and again when both use it 95% of the time. You need each annotator's own marginals, not just the class balance — write down why a single "class balance" figure does not determine $p_e$, and construct two tables with the same balance and different kappas. Then explain the difference to someone who believes 90% agreement is 90% agreement.
3. Reproduce the random-100 audit on a dataset of your own. Classify each row as error, undecidable, or ok, using criteria you write down *before* you start reading. Report the counts and the rule-of-three upper bound.
4. Reproduce the noise-direction experiment on a *balanced* dataset. Does the asymmetry between the two directions survive? Explain the result from the class counts, as this chapter did.
5. Build a second annotator for a task of your own — a lexicon, a regex, or an LLM prompt. Compute kappa against the gold labels, then compute it again on a class-balanced subsample. Report both, and say which one you would put in a paper.
6. Run the out-of-fold flagging procedure on your own training set. Read the twenty highest-confidence flags. Classify each as error, schema, or model. Then retrain with them dropped and with them flipped, and report whether either helped.
7. Take a benchmark result you believe — yours or a published one — and audit it for all six kinds of leakage listed in @sec-leakage. Report which checks you could actually perform and which you could not.
8. Using the budget grid, compute the break-even error rate at which 5,000 labels beat 40,000: the noise level where the 5,000-row clean score equals the 40,000-row noisy score. Then argue, with the numbers, for how a team with a fixed budget should split it between training and test annotation.
